questions.stem: A 28-year-old farmer presents with sudden-onset diplopia, dysphagia, and descending flaccid paralysis after consuming home-canned vegetables. He is afebrile and alert. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Botulism presents with descending flaccid paralysis due to preformed neurotoxin, often from improperly canned foods.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old student develops bloody diarrhea, fever, and abdominal cramps 24 hours after eating undercooked chicken at a barbecue. Stool culture reveals Gram-negative, oxidase-positive, curved rods. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Campylobacter jejuni is a Gram-negative, oxidase-positive, curved rod commonly associated with undercooked poultry.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with sickle cell disease presents with acute right knee pain, fever, and swelling. Blood cultures are pending. Which organism is most likely responsible for his osteomyelitis?
questions.explanation: Salmonella spp. are the most common cause of osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease due to functional asplenia.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with multiple painless, skin-colored papules on her vulva and perianal area. Some lesions are cauliflower-shaped. Which human papillomavirus (HPV) type is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: HPV-6 and HPV-11 are most commonly associated with anogenital warts (condyloma acuminata).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is bitten by a stray dog in Nairobi. He has no prior rabies vaccination. Which post-exposure prophylaxis regimen is most appropriate?
options: Five doses of IM rabies vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28
Five doses of IM rabies vaccine plus human rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound
Human rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound only
questions.answer: Five doses of IM rabies vaccine plus human rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound
questions.explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis for rabies requires both rabies vaccine and human rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with 5 days of watery diarrhea, vomiting, and fever. He is moderately dehydrated. Which adjunctive therapy has been shown to reduce the duration and severity of diarrhea in this age group?
questions.explanation: Zinc supplementation reduces the duration and severity of diarrhea in children, particularly in resource-limited settings.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with fever, right knee pain, and swelling. Joint aspiration reveals purulent fluid with Gram-negative diplococci. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Gonococcal septic arthritis is characterized by Gram-negative diplococci in joint fluid and is common in sexually active young adults.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with migratory swellings over her arm and back, lasting 1–3 days. She recently returned from Cameroon. Which vector is most likely responsible for her infection?
questions.explanation: Chrysops deerfly is the vector for Loa loa, a filarial nematode causing loiasis.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy presents with acute osteomyelitis of the distal tibia. Blood cultures are pending. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Empirical therapy for acute osteomyelitis should cover Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Gram-negative organisms.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with cholera-like symptoms after consuming contaminated water. Which mechanism best describes the action of the cholera toxin?
options: ADP ribosylation of inhibitory G proteins leading to reduced cAMP
ADP ribosylation of stimulatory G proteins leading to elevated intracellular cAMP
Formation of cation-selective pores in cell membranes
questions.answer: ADP ribosylation of stimulatory G proteins leading to elevated intracellular cAMP
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the stimulatory Gs protein, leading to persistent activation of adenylate cyclase and elevated cAMP.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with acute hematogenous osteomyelitis of the distal femur. After 3 days of IV antibiotics, he remains febrile with persistent pain. Imaging reveals a 1.5 cm abscess. Which laboratory parameter is most useful for monitoring early treatment response?
questions.explanation: CRP is a sensitive marker for early response to treatment in osteomyelitis, with levels declining within 48–72 hours of effective therapy.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes presents with a dog bite wound to his leg. He is allergic to sulfa drugs. Which antibiotic is most appropriate for prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin-clavulanate covers Pasteurella multocida and other oral flora. Tetanus toxoid should be administered if the patient's vaccination status is uncertain.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with a 1-week history of cramping abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Stool culture is positive for Campylobacter jejuni. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Azithromycin is the preferred agent for Campylobacter jejuni enteritis, particularly in severe or prolonged cases.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with sudden-onset fever, fatigue, and inability to bear weight on the right leg. Examination reveals swelling and point tenderness over the proximal tibia. Which imaging modality is most sensitive for early diagnosis?
questions.explanation: MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for early diagnosis of osteomyelitis, detecting changes within 24–48 hours.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man presents with fever, joint pain, and a petechial rash after returning from a trip to Mombasa. He is sexually active. Which organism is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Disseminated gonococcal infection can present with fever, joint pain, and petechial rash, particularly in sexually active individuals.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with fever, confusion, and a new rash on her chest after returning from a trip to Mathare slums. Blood cultures are pending. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Typhoid fever presents with fever, confusion, and rash (rose spots), often after travel to endemic areas.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with sudden-onset fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture reveals turbid CSF with elevated neutrophils and low glucose. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Neisseria meningitidis is a common cause of bacterial meningitis in adolescents and young adults, presenting with fever, headache, and neck stiffness.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and rust-colored sputum. Chest X-ray shows lobar consolidation. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia with lobar consolidation.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl presents with intense perianal itching and irritability. Eggs with a flattened side are identified on scotch tape test. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) causes perianal itching and is diagnosed by identifying eggs on scotch tape test.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain after returning from a trip to the Maasai Mara. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Leptospirosis presents with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain (Weil's syndrome) after exposure to contaminated water.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with fever, joint pain, and a macular rash after a tick bite. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Rickettsia rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever, characterized by fever, rash, and joint pain after a tick bite.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and weight loss after returning from a trip to Uganda. Chest X-ray shows miliary pattern. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Miliary tuberculosis presents with fever, cough, weight loss, and a miliary pattern on chest X-ray, often after travel to endemic areas.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with fever, headache, and photophobia after swimming in Lake Victoria. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Naegleria fowleri causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis, often after swimming in warm freshwater.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with fever, abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked beef. Stool culture reveals Gram-negative, oxidase-negative rods. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Escherichia coli O157:H7 causes hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome after consuming undercooked beef.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with fever, cough, and night sweats after returning from a trip to the Rift Valley. Chest X-ray shows upper lobe cavitation. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis presents with fever, cough, night sweats, and upper lobe cavitation on chest X-ray, often after travel to endemic areas.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture reveals clear CSF with elevated lymphocytes and normal glucose. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Enteroviruses are the most common cause of aseptic meningitis, presenting with lymphocytic pleocytosis and normal glucose.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and rust-colored sputum. Chest X-ray shows lobar consolidation. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Empirical therapy for community-acquired pneumonia should cover Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical organisms (e.g., Mycoplasma pneumoniae).

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with fever, dysuria, and flank pain. Urinalysis reveals pyuria and bacteriuria. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Escherichia coli is the most common cause of urinary tract infections, including pyelonephritis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and weight loss after returning from a trip to Ethiopia. Chest X-ray shows a solitary pulmonary nodule. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Histoplasmosis presents with fever, cough, weight loss, and a solitary pulmonary nodule, often after exposure to bird or bat droppings.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain after returning from a trip to the Maasai Mara. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Empirical therapy for leptospirosis includes IV ceftriaxone or doxycycline, depending on severity.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with fever, joint pain, and a macular rash after a tick bite. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Doxycycline is the drug of choice for Rocky Mountain spotted fever, a rickettsial infection transmitted by ticks.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with fever, confusion, and a new rash on her chest after returning from a trip to Mathare slums. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Empirical therapy for typhoid fever includes IV ceftriaxone, with azithromycin as an alternative in penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with fever, abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked beef. Stool culture reveals Gram-negative, oxidase-negative rods. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Azithromycin is the preferred agent for enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC) infections, though antimicrobials are generally avoided in EHEC to prevent hemolytic uremic syndrome.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and weight loss after returning from a trip to the Rift Valley. Chest X-ray shows upper lobe cavitation. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
options: IV Isoniazid + IV Rifampicin + IV Pyrazinamide + IV Ethambutol
questions.answer: IV Isoniazid + IV Rifampicin + IV Pyrazinamide + IV Ethambutol
questions.explanation: Empirical therapy for tuberculosis includes a four-drug regimen (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) until susceptibility results are available.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture reveals clear CSF with elevated lymphocytes and normal glucose. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Acyclovir is the drug of choice for herpes simplex virus encephalitis, a common cause of aseptic meningitis with lymphocytic pleocytosis.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with fever, dysuria, and flank pain. Urinalysis reveals pyuria and bacteriuria. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone with excellent urinary penetration and is commonly used for pyelonephritis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and weight loss after returning from a trip to Ethiopia. Chest X-ray shows a solitary pulmonary nodule. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Itraconazole is the drug of choice for histoplasmosis, a fungal infection common in endemic areas.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with sudden-onset fever, fatigue, and pain in his right lower leg. He is no longer able to bear weight. Examination reveals swelling, point tenderness over the proximal tibia, and limited movement. Labs: Hb 12.5 g/dL, WBC 15,000/mm³, ESR 65 mm/h. Bone scan shows increased uptake at the metaphysis of the tibia.

modelAnswer.a: Most likely diagnosis: Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis of the proximal tibia.
modelAnswer.b: Pharmacological management: Empirical IV antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus (e.g., IV Vancomycin + IV Ceftriaxone) for at least 4–6 weeks. Consider de-escalation based on culture results.
modelAnswer.c: Non-pharmacological management: Rest, elevation of the limb, and analgesia (e.g., paracetamol or ibuprofen). Surgical debridement may be required if there is abscess formation or failure to improve clinically.
modelAnswer.d: Monitoring: Serial CRP and ESR to assess response to therapy. Repeat imaging (MRI or bone scan) if clinical deterioration occurs.

questions.stem: Identify the most important member of Enterobacteriaceae that causes each of the following diseases:

modelAnswer.a: Childhood diarrhea: Escherichia coli (enteropathogenic E. coli, EPEC).
modelAnswer.b: Traveler's diarrhea: Escherichia coli (enterotoxigenic E. coli, ETEC).
modelAnswer.d: Hemorrhagic colitis or Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS): Escherichia coli O157:H7 (enterohemorrhagic E. coli, EHEC).

questions.stem: Identify 3 human worms (parasites) that can cause iron deficiency anemia and 1 parasite associated with pernicious anemia.

modelAnswer.b: Parasite associated with pernicious anemia: Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm, causes vitamin B12 deficiency).

questions.stem: Pablo, a 41-year-old security officer, is bitten by a neighbor’s dog while passing near the neighbor’s driveway. The dog’s vaccination history is unclear. Formulate an appropriate treatment plan for Pablo and include counseling points.

modelAnswer.i: Avoid contact with the dog and seek medical attention if symptoms of rabies (e.g., fever, confusion, hydrophobia) develop.
modelAnswer.ii: Complete the full course of rabies vaccine and HRIG to ensure protection.
modelAnswer.iii: Monitor the wound for signs of infection (e.g., redness, swelling, pus) and seek medical attention if these occur.
modelAnswer.iv: Follow up with a healthcare provider for wound check and further counseling.

questions.stem: Match each clinical presentation with the causative parasite:

modelAnswer.a: Migratory swellings lasting 1–3 days: Loa loa.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with fever, joint pain, and a petechial rash after returning from a trip to Mombasa. He is sexually active. Labs: Hb 13.6 g/L, WBC 13.4 x10⁶/µL, CRP 318, ESR 96. What should be your working diagnosis?

modelAnswer.b: Justification: Fever, joint pain, petechial rash, and elevated inflammatory markers are consistent with DGI, particularly in a sexually active individual.

questions.stem: Select the most common organism causing osteomyelitis in children under 3 years.
Which of the following statements is CORRECT regarding Vibrio cholerae infection?

modelAnswer.a: The organism is isolated from a stool sample (not blood).
modelAnswer.b: The natural reservoir of the organism is environmental water sources (not domestic animals).
modelAnswer.c: The LPS complex is a virulence factor, but the main virulence factor is the cholera toxin (an enterotoxin).
modelAnswer.d: The correct statement: An enterotoxin is the main virulence factor.

Social history: recently traveled to Mwea for a family function. Rest of the physical examination is normal.

modelAnswer.ii: Use mosquito bite prevention measures (e.g., insecticide-treated bed nets, repellents) to avoid future infections.
modelAnswer.iii: Monitor the child for signs of worsening illness (e.g., persistent vomiting, seizures, altered consciousness) and seek medical attention immediately if these occur.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old farmer presents with progressive weakness of his upper limbs over 48 hours, followed by descending paralysis. He reports no fever but has diplopia and dysphagia. He recently consumed home-canned beans. Which toxin is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Descending flaccid paralysis with preserved consciousness and no fever is classic for botulism, typically from preformed toxin in improperly preserved foods.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old student develops bloody diarrhea 3 days after eating undercooked chicken at a campus barbecue. Stool culture confirms Campylobacter jejuni. Which antimicrobial is first-line for this infection?
questions.explanation: Azithromycin is the preferred agent for Campylobacter enteritis due to high resistance rates to fluoroquinolones in many regions.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child with sickle cell disease presents with acute right knee pain and fever. Blood cultures grow Salmonella species. Which organism is most likely responsible for his osteomyelitis?
questions.explanation: Salmonella is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease due to functional asplenia and impaired opsonization.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man returns from a safari in Maasai Mara with migratory swellings on his arm that last 2–3 days. He recalls being bitten by flies. Which vector is most likely responsible for his infection?
questions.explanation: Chrysops deerflies transmit Loa loa, causing loiasis characterized by Calabar swellings and microfilariae in blood.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with fever, confusion, and a new macular rash on her trunk 10 days after returning from a rural area with poor sanitation. Blood cultures are pending. Which organism is most likely causing her typhoid fever?
questions.explanation: Typhoid fever presents with fever, confusion, and rash (rose spots) after exposure to contaminated food/water in endemic areas.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy develops sudden onset of fever, joint pain, and a pustular rash on his arms 48 hours after a camping trip. He is sexually active. Which organism is most likely responsible for his septic arthritis?
questions.explanation: Gonococcal arthritis typically presents with fever, tenosynovitis, and pustular skin lesions in sexually active individuals.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with acute watery diarrhea (>15 stools/day) and signs of severe dehydration is admitted. Stool culture confirms Vibrio cholerae. Which mechanism explains the profuse diarrhea?
options: ADP-ribosylation of stimulatory G proteins increasing cAMP
Formation of cation-selective pores in enterocytes
questions.answer: ADP-ribosylation of stimulatory G proteins increasing cAMP
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs proteins, permanently activating adenylate cyclase and increasing cAMP, leading to chloride secretion and watery diarrhea.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with multiple painless, cauliflower-like lesions on her vulva. HPV typing confirms HPV-6. Which clinical syndrome is most likely?
questions.explanation: HPV-6 and HPV-11 are low-risk types causing anogenital warts (condyloma acuminata), while high-risk types (16, 18) cause neoplasia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man sustains a dog bite to his hand while traveling in a rabies-endemic area. He has no prior rabies vaccination. Which post-exposure prophylaxis regimen is indicated?
options: Rabies vaccine plus human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) infiltrated into the wound
HRIG alone infiltrated into the wound
No prophylaxis needed if wound is clean
questions.answer: Rabies vaccine plus human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) infiltrated into the wound
questions.explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis for rabies requires both rabies vaccine (days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28) and HRIG infiltrated into the wound to neutralize virus at the inoculation site.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with 5 days of watery diarrhea, vomiting, and fever is admitted with severe dehydration. Which adjunctive therapy improves outcomes?
questions.explanation: Zinc reduces duration and severity of diarrhea in children, especially in resource-limited settings, by enhancing intestinal repair and immune function.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with acute hematogenous osteomyelitis of the tibia shows no clinical improvement after 3 days of IV cloxacillin. Imaging reveals a 2 cm abscess. Which laboratory marker is most useful for monitoring early treatment response?
questions.explanation: CRP rises rapidly with infection and normalizes faster than ESR, making it the most expeditious marker for early treatment response in osteomyelitis.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man presents with fever, right knee swelling, and pain after a soccer injury. Joint aspirate shows >50,000 WBC/mm³ with 90% neutrophils. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of septic arthritis in adults, often following trauma or hematogenous spread.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes presents with a dog bite wound to his leg that is erythematous, swollen, and tender. Which antimicrobial is most appropriate for empiric therapy?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin-clavulanate provides coverage against Pasteurella multocida (common in dog bites) and oral anaerobes, making it first-line for bite wounds.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with fever, irritability, and refusal to bear weight on the right leg. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Which empirical IV antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Cloxacillin (or nafcillin) is first-line for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus osteomyelitis in children due to excellent bone penetration.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child develops sudden onset of fever, bloody diarrhea, and oliguria 3 days after eating undercooked beef. Stool culture confirms E. coli O157:H7. Which complication is most likely?
questions.explanation: E. coli O157:H7 produces Shiga toxin causing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury (HUS).

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with fever, migratory arthralgias, and a petechial rash after returning from a hiking trip. Blood cultures are pending. Which organism is most likely responsible for her disseminated infection?
questions.explanation: Leptospirosis presents with fever, myalgias, conjunctival suffusion, and rash after exposure to contaminated water, especially in tropical regions.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy presents with fever, sore throat, and a grayish pseudomembrane on his tonsils. Which organism is responsible for his diphtheria?
questions.explanation: Diphtheria is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, producing an exotoxin leading to pseudomembrane formation and systemic toxicity.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl presents with intense perianal itching and irritability. Scotch tape test reveals flattened eggs. Which organism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) causes perianal itching, especially at night, with flattened eggs visible on scotch tape test.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with fever, jaundice, and dark urine 2 weeks after returning from a rural area. Which organism is most likely responsible for his leptospirosis?
questions.explanation: Leptospirosis presents with fever, jaundice (Weil's syndrome), and renal failure after exposure to contaminated water or soil.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder presents with fever, cough, and foul-smelling sputum. Chest X-ray shows a lung abscess. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Lung abscesses in alcoholics are often polymicrobial, with anaerobic bacteria (e.g., Bacteroides, Fusobacterium) being predominant.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with fever, dysuria, and flank pain. Urine culture grows Escherichia coli. Which virulence factor is most important for her ascending urinary tract infection?
questions.explanation: P fimbriae (P adhesins) mediate attachment to uroepithelial cells, enabling ascending infection in the urinary tract.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with fever, cough, and wheezing. Nasopharyngeal aspirate confirms respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Which antiviral is indicated?
questions.explanation: RSV infection in infants is managed supportively; ribavirin is rarely used due to limited efficacy and toxicity.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with fever, headache, and a macular rash on his wrists and ankles after a camping trip. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) presents with fever, headache, and petechial rash after tick bite, caused by Rickettsia rickettsii.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, and a sandpaper-like rash. Which organism is responsible for his scarlet fever?
questions.explanation: Scarlet fever is caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus) producing pyrogenic exotoxins leading to rash and strawberry tongue.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with fever, arthralgias, and a target lesion (erythema migrans) after a hiking trip. Which organism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Lyme disease (early localized stage) presents with erythema migrans, fever, and arthralgias after Ixodes tick bite.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with diabetes presents with a painful, swollen right ear canal and fever. Which organism is most likely responsible for his malignant otitis externa?
questions.explanation: Malignant otitis externa in diabetics is typically caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, requiring prolonged IV antipseudomonal therapy.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and hemoptysis 3 weeks after returning from a rural area. Chest X-ray shows upper lobe cavitation. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Post-primary tuberculosis presents with upper lobe cavitary lesions, fever, and hemoptysis after reactivation of latent infection.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with fever, confusion, and a new macular rash on her trunk 10 days after returning from a rural area with poor sanitation. Blood cultures grow Salmonella Typhi. Which complication is most likely?
questions.explanation: Typhoid fever complications include intestinal perforation (especially in the ileum) due to Peyer's patch necrosis, presenting with peritonitis.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with fever, cough, and wheezing. Nasopharyngeal aspirate confirms Bordetella pertussis. Which antimicrobial is indicated?
questions.explanation: Azithromycin is first-line for pertussis, reducing transmission and severity if given early in the catarrhal phase.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with fever, dysuria, and a purulent urethral discharge. Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci. Which organism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Gonorrhea presents with purulent urethritis; gram-negative diplococci on Gram stain are diagnostic for Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with COPD presents with fever, cough, and purulent sputum. Chest X-ray shows a right lower lobe infiltrate. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia, including in COPD patients.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, vomiting, and a stiff neck. Lumbar puncture shows CSF with 500 WBC/mm³ (90% neutrophils), low glucose, and high protein. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Meningococcal meningitis presents with acute onset of fever, meningismus, and CSF findings of low glucose and high protein with neutrophilic pleocytosis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with fever, cough, and rust-colored sputum. Chest X-ray shows a right middle lobe consolidation. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of lobar pneumonia with rust-colored sputum due to alveolar hemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and night sweats 3 weeks after returning from a rural area. Chest X-ray shows hilar lymphadenopathy. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Histoplasmosis presents with fever, cough, and hilar lymphadenopathy after exposure to bird/bat droppings in endemic areas.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, and a 'strawberry tongue.' Which organism is responsible for his scarlet fever?
questions.explanation: Scarlet fever is caused by Streptococcus pyogenes producing pyrogenic exotoxins, leading to 'strawberry tongue' and sandpaper rash.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and hemoptysis 2 months after returning from a rural area. Chest X-ray shows a solitary pulmonary nodule. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Coccidioidomycosis presents with fever, cough, and pulmonary nodules after exposure to soil in endemic Southwestern U.S. regions.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with sickle cell disease presents with fever and right knee pain. Blood cultures grow Salmonella species. a) Identify the most likely diagnosis. b) Outline the pharmacological management (include dose and duration). c) List two non-pharmacological interventions.
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Acute osteomyelitis due to Salmonella species.

b) Pharmacological management:
- IV ceftriaxone 75 mg/kg once daily (max 2 g/day) for 4–6 weeks, followed by oral ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg twice daily (max 500 mg/dose) for 2–4 weeks to complete 6 weeks total therapy.
- Analgesia: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg/dose every 6 hours as needed (max 60 mg/kg/day).

c) Non-pharmacological interventions:
- Immobilization of the affected limb with a splint to reduce pain and prevent pathological fractures.
- Physical therapy after acute phase to restore function and prevent contractures.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with fever, joint pain, and a petechial rash after returning from a hiking trip. Blood cultures are pending. a) Identify the most likely diagnosis. b) List three diagnostic tests to confirm the diagnosis. c) Outline the empirical antimicrobial therapy.
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Leptospirosis.

b) Diagnostic tests:
- Serum microscopic agglutination test (MAT) for Leptospira antibodies (gold standard).
- PCR for Leptospira DNA in blood or urine (early phase).
- Dark-field microscopy of urine for leptospires (less sensitive).

c) Empirical antimicrobial therapy:
- IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units every 6 hours for 7 days OR
- IV doxycycline 200 mg once daily for 7 days (if penicillin-allergic).

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with fever, cough, and wheezing. Nasopharyngeal aspirate confirms respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). a) Outline the supportive care for this patient. b) List two high-risk groups for severe RSV infection. c) When is palivizumab prophylaxis indicated?
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Supportive care:
- Oxygen therapy if SpO2 <90%.
- Hydration with oral or IV fluids as needed.
- Antipyretics (paracetamol 15 mg/kg/dose every 6 hours) for fever.
- Nebulized 3% saline to improve mucus clearance (optional).

b) High-risk groups for severe RSV infection:
- Premature infants (<35 weeks gestation).
- Infants with chronic lung disease (e.g., bronchopulmonary dysplasia).

c) Palivizumab prophylaxis is indicated for:
- Infants born at <29 weeks gestation during their first RSV season.
- Infants with hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease or chronic lung disease of prematurity.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, bloody diarrhea, and oliguria 3 days after eating undercooked beef. Stool culture confirms E. coli O157:H7. a) Identify the most likely complication. b) Outline the management of this complication. c) List two preventive measures for this infection.
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).

b) Management of HUS:
- Supportive care: Fluid and electrolyte balance, blood pressure control, and dialysis if indicated (e.g., severe hyperkalemia, uremia, or fluid overload).
- Avoid antimotility agents and antibiotics (may increase toxin release and worsen HUS).
- Transfusion if severe anemia or thrombocytopenia.

c) Preventive measures:
- Cook beef thoroughly to an internal temperature of 71°C (160°F).
- Avoid unpasteurized dairy products and contaminated water.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man presents with fever, dysuria, and a purulent urethral discharge. Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci. a) Identify the organism responsible. b) Outline the first-line antimicrobial therapy (include dose and duration). c) List two complications if untreated.
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

b) First-line antimicrobial therapy:
- Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM as a single dose (if <150 kg) OR 1 g IM if ≥150 kg.
- If chlamydial co-infection is suspected (common), add azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose OR doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days.

c) Complications if untreated:
- Disseminated gonococcal infection (e.g., septic arthritis, tenosynovitis, dermatitis).
- Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) in women, leading to infertility or ectopic pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with fever, confusion, and a new macular rash on her trunk 10 days after returning from a rural area with poor sanitation. Blood cultures grow Salmonella Typhi. a) Identify the most likely diagnosis. b) Outline the antimicrobial therapy (include dose and duration). c) List two preventive measures.
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Typhoid fever.

b) Antimicrobial therapy:
- First-line: Oral azithromycin 1 g once daily for 5–7 days OR
- IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily for 10–14 days (if severe or unable to tolerate oral therapy).
- Alternative: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7–10 days (if local resistance patterns allow).

c) Preventive measures:
- Safe food and water practices (boil water, avoid raw vegetables, peel fruits).
- Typhoid vaccination (inactivated or live oral) for travelers to endemic areas.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, and a sandpaper-like rash. a) Identify the organism responsible. b) Outline the first-line antimicrobial therapy (include dose and duration). c) List two complications if untreated.
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus).

b) First-line antimicrobial therapy:
- Oral penicillin V 250 mg twice daily (children) or 500 mg twice daily (adults) for 10 days.
- Alternative: Amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day divided into two doses for 10 days (max 1 g/day).
- If penicillin-allergic: Azithromycin 12 mg/kg once daily for 5 days (max 500 mg/day).

c) Complications if untreated:
- Rheumatic fever (acute rheumatic carditis, arthritis, chorea).
- Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and hemoptysis 3 weeks after returning from a rural area. Chest X-ray shows upper lobe cavitation. a) Identify the most likely diagnosis. b) Outline the diagnostic tests to confirm the diagnosis. c) List two first-line antimicrobial agents.
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Post-primary pulmonary tuberculosis.

b) Diagnostic tests:
- Sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture (gold standard).
- GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay for rapid detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance.
- Chest X-ray (shows upper lobe cavitation).
- Tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) for latent TB screening.

c) First-line antimicrobial agents (RIPE regimen):
- Rifampicin 10 mg/kg/day (max 600 mg/day) for 6 months.
- Isoniazid 5 mg/kg/day (max 300 mg/day) for 6 months.
- Pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg/day (max 2 g/day) for 2 months.
- Ethambutol 15 mg/kg/day (max 1.2 g/day) for 2 months.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old obese woman presents to the emergency department with a 1-week history of fever, confusion, and delirium. She also reports abdominal pain, headache, and anorexia. One day before admission, she noted a new, red macular rash on her chest. Her history is significant for returning 10 days ago from Mathare slums, where she stayed with relatives recovering from typhoid fever. Admission vital signs: temperature 38.3°C, heart rate 60 bpm, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. Physical examination reveals splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests: WBC 3.0 × 10⁶/μL, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, platelets 120 × 10³/μL, ALT 85 U/L, AST 90 U/L, ALP 150 U/L, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL. Blood cultures are pending.

a) Identify the most likely presumptive diagnosis and the probable causative agent. (2 marks)
b) Why is her history of present illness, clinical presentation, and laboratory results consistent with this diagnosis? Provide four points (1 mark each).
c) Illustrate three benefits of antimicrobial treatment in this patient. (3 marks)
d) Design an appropriate treatment plan for this patient (include adjunctive and supportive therapy). (5 marks)

Fourteen months after discharge from the hospital, the patient’s stool is still positive for the same microbial agent. Propose four therapeutic options that are available to cure her chronic carrier state. (4 marks)

e) Outline two preventive measures against this condition. (2 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Presumptive diagnosis: Typhoid fever. Causative agent: Salmonella Typhi.

b) Consistency with diagnosis:
1. Exposure history: Returned from an endemic area (Mathare slums) where typhoid is prevalent, with close contact to cases.
2. Clinical presentation: Fever, confusion (encephalopathy), abdominal pain, and a macular rash (rose spots) are classic for typhoid fever.
3. Laboratory findings: Leukopenia (WBC 3.0 × 10⁶/μL) is typical in typhoid fever due to bone marrow suppression; mild transaminitis (ALT/AST elevation) reflects hepatic involvement.
4. Splenomegaly and hepatomegaly: Reflect reticuloendothelial system involvement in typhoid infection.

c) Benefits of antimicrobial treatment:
1. Reduces mortality: Early treatment reduces the case fatality rate from ~10–30% (untreated) to <1%.
2. Shortens duration of illness: Symptoms resolve within 3–5 days of appropriate therapy (vs. 3–4 weeks untreated).
3. Prevents complications: Reduces risk of intestinal perforation, hemorrhage, and chronic carriage.


d) Treatment plan:
- Antimicrobial therapy: Oral azithromycin 1 g once daily for 7 days (preferred for uncomplicated typhoid in regions with fluoroquinolone resistance).
- Supportive care: IV fluids (normal saline) for dehydration; antipyretics (paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours as needed) for fever.
- Monitoring: Daily vital signs, CBC, liver function tests, and blood cultures (if available).
- Adjunctive therapy: Nutritional support (high-calorie, high-protein diet) to aid recovery.
- Infection control: Standard precautions; educate patient on hygiene to prevent transmission.


e) Preventive measures:
1. Safe food and water practices: Boil drinking water, avoid raw vegetables, peel fruits, and consume well-cooked food.
2. Typhoid vaccination: Administer the Vi polysaccharide vaccine (inactivated) or live oral Ty21a vaccine before travel to endemic areas.

questions.stem:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the outpatient department by his mother. She reports that he was well until this morning when he woke up feeling tired and vomited after breakfast. His mother noted he felt hot and gave him a half tablet of paracetamol. On examination, he is alert, well-nourished (20 kg), not pale, and has an axillary temperature of 38.5°C. Social history reveals they recently traveled to Mwea for a family function. The rest of the physical examination is normal.

a) Identify the most likely diagnosis and causative agent. (2 marks)

b) Justify your answer in (a) above with four points (0.5 marks each).

c) Propose three diagnostic tests that would help confirm your diagnosis and elaborate on their utility. (3 marks)

d) Compile an elaborate treatment plan for this patient (include the dosing regimen for all pharmacological agents). (4 marks)

e) Illustrate three counselling points that you would offer the mother regarding treatment. (3 marks)

The patient is brought back later in the night. The mother reports that the boy has not been retaining anything. He has refused food but has drunk a little. The mother says the child had a 'fit' late afternoon; he regained consciousness immediately. For the past few hours, the child has been increasingly drowsy and has now become unconscious. At examination, the child is well-nourished, unconscious, and not dehydrated. Axillary temperature is 40.2°C; pulse rate 120/min (regular); blood pressure 90/70 mmHg. There is no neck stiffness or rash. Pupils are equal; a few retinal hemorrhages are seen; no papilloedema. Some yellowish sticky fluid is seen filling the left external auditory meatus. Reflexes are normal.

f) Identify the most probable diagnosis and justify your answer. (2 marks)

g) Design an appropriate treatment plan for this patient. (4 marks)

A 28-year-old man presents with sudden onset of blurred vision, dry mouth, and descending flaccid paralysis 6 hours after eating home-canned beans. He denies fever or altered mental status. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Botulism presents with descending flaccid paralysis due to preformed neurotoxin; foodborne botulism follows ingestion of preformed toxin in improperly canned foods.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child develops severe pharyngitis with a thick, gray pseudomembrane on the tonsils and anterior pharynx. The child is afebrile but appears toxic. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.explanation: Diphtheria is characterized by a pseudomembrane in the throat and systemic toxicity; caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae producing diphtheria toxin.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old farmer presents with trismus, risus sardonicus, and generalized muscle spasms 10 days after stepping on a rusty nail. He is afebrile and alert. The most appropriate initial management is:
options: Tetanus immunoglobulin 3000 IU IM plus Tdap vaccine
Diazepam 5–10 mg IV for muscle spasms
Penicillin G 2 million units IV q4h
questions.answer: Tetanus immunoglobulin 3000 IU IM plus Tdap vaccine
questions.explanation: Tetanus management includes passive immunization with tetanus immunoglobulin and active immunization with tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine; benzodiazepines are adjunctive for spasms.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old student develops bloody diarrhea and severe abdominal cramps 3 days after eating undercooked chicken at a barbecue. Stool culture grows oxidase-positive, curved, gram-negative rods. The most likely organism is:
questions.explanation: Campylobacter jejuni is oxidase-positive, curved, gram-negative bacillus causing bloody diarrhea after poultry exposure; commonly isolated from stool cultures.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with 10 days of profuse, rice-water diarrhea after drinking untreated water during a rural trek. Stool microscopy shows no fecal leukocytes. The likely mechanism of action of the causative toxin is:
options: ADP-ribosylation of stimulatory Gs protein leading to increased cAMP
Formation of cation-selective pores in enterocyte membranes
Inhibition of sodium-glucose cotransporter in the gut
questions.answer: ADP-ribosylation of stimulatory Gs protein leading to increased cAMP
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the stimulatory Gs protein, locking it in the active state and causing persistent elevation of intracellular cAMP, leading to massive chloride and water secretion.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with sickle cell disease presents with acute onset of fever and right knee pain. Imaging reveals osteomyelitis of the distal femur. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.explanation: In sickle cell disease, Salmonella is the most common cause of osteomyelitis due to functional asplenia and impaired opsonization.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with acute monoarthritis of the knee, fever, and a pustular rash on his arms. Synovial fluid analysis shows 50,000 WBC/mm³ with 90% neutrophils. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.explanation: Gonococcal arthritis is common in sexually active adults and presents with monoarthritis, tenosynovitis, and pustular rash; synovial fluid shows high neutrophil count.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with 5 days of watery diarrhea, vomiting, and fever after attending a daycare center. The child is moderately dehydrated. In addition to oral rehydration solution, the most beneficial adjunctive therapy is:
questions.explanation: Zinc supplementation reduces duration and severity of acute diarrhea in children, especially in resource-limited settings; WHO recommends 20 mg/day for 10–14 days.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman presents with multiple painless, skin-colored papules on her vulva and perianal area that have coalesced into cauliflower-like clusters. The most likely HPV type associated with these lesions is:
questions.explanation: HPV-6 and HPV-11 are low-risk types associated with anogenital warts (condyloma acuminata), while HPV-16 and 18 are high-risk types linked to cervical cancer.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is bitten by a stray dog on his forearm while hiking in Laikipia. The dog is unavailable for observation. The patient has completed a primary tetanus series and received a booster 8 years ago. The most appropriate post-exposure rabies prophylaxis includes:
options: Rabies vaccine alone on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28
Rabies vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28 plus human rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound
Human rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound only
No rabies prophylaxis needed if wound is cleaned
questions.answer: Rabies vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28 plus human rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound
questions.explanation: For category III exposures (bites or scratches), both rabies vaccine (5 doses) and human rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound are indicated.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with migratory swellings on her arm and back that last 2–3 days, accompanied by pruritus and warmth. She recently returned from a 6-month stay in Cameroon. The most likely vector for her infection is:
questions.explanation: Loiasis is transmitted by the Chrysops deerfly; characterized by Calabar swellings and microfilariae in blood.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with acute hematogenous osteomyelitis of the distal tibia. After 3 days of IV cloxacillin, he remains febrile with persistent pain. Imaging reveals a 2 cm subperiosteal abscess. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Continue IV antibiotics and reassess in 48 hours
Switch to oral antibiotics and discharge
questions.explanation: Surgical drainage is indicated for subperiosteal abscess in acute osteomyelitis not responding to 48–72 hours of appropriate IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with fever, right knee pain, and swelling 3 days after a minor knee injury. Synovial fluid shows 80,000 WBC/mm³ with 95% neutrophils. Blood cultures are pending. The most appropriate empiric antibiotic is:
questions.explanation: Empiric therapy for septic arthritis should cover Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) with vancomycin until culture results are available.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old student develops cramping abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea 2 days after returning from a camping trip. Stool culture grows Campylobacter jejuni. The most appropriate antimicrobial therapy is:
options: Azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily for 3 days
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO twice daily for 7 days
Metronidazole 500 mg PO three times daily for 7 days
questions.answer: Azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily for 3 days
questions.explanation: Azithromycin is the preferred agent for Campylobacter enteritis due to increasing resistance to fluoroquinolones; duration is typically 3 days.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old diabetic man presents with a dog bite to his hand that is erythematous, swollen, and tender. He has no signs of systemic infection. He is allergic to sulfa drugs. The most appropriate empiric oral antibiotic is:
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin-clavulanate provides coverage for Pasteurella multocida and oral anaerobes; safe in sulfa-allergic patients.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, irritability, and refusal to bear weight on the right leg. Examination reveals localized warmth and tenderness over the distal femur. X-ray is normal. The most sensitive early diagnostic test is:
questions.explanation: MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for early detection of osteomyelitis, showing bone marrow edema within 24–48 hours of onset.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with fever, fatigue, and pain in his right hip after a soccer game. He has limited internal rotation and pain on palpation of the greater trochanter. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Transient synovitis is the most common cause of acute hip pain in children, often post-viral or post-trauma, with normal or mildly elevated inflammatory markers.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with fever, migratory polyarthritis, and a pustular rash on her palms and soles. She is sexually active with multiple partners. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Disseminated gonococcal infection presents with fever, tenosynovitis, migratory polyarthritis, and pustular rash; strongly associated with sexual activity.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with sudden onset of fever, vomiting, and profuse watery diarrhea after eating reheated rice. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.explanation: Bacillus cereus causes emetic-type food poisoning within 1–6 hours of ingesting reheated rice contaminated with heat-stable toxin.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with severe watery diarrhea, vomiting, and signs of dehydration. Stool microscopy shows no fecal leukocytes. The most appropriate initial rehydration strategy is:
options: Oral rehydration solution with low osmolarity
questions.answer: Oral rehydration solution with low osmolarity
questions.explanation: Oral rehydration solution with low osmolarity is the WHO-recommended first-line therapy for dehydration due to acute gastroenteritis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with fever, headache, and diarrhea 1 week after returning from a trip to rural Western Kenya. He reports exposure to stagnant water. The most likely parasitic cause of his symptoms is:
questions.explanation: Schistosomiasis (bilharzia) is acquired through skin contact with freshwater containing cercariae; causes acute febrile illness (Katayama fever) and later hepatic/intestinal disease.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with fever, confusion, and a new macular rash on her trunk 10 days after returning from a rural area. She reports exposure to ticks. Blood smear shows intraerythrocytic parasites. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Malaria presents with fever, confusion, and rash after travel to endemic areas; diagnosis confirmed by identification of Plasmodium parasites on blood smear.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with intense perianal itching and irritability. Scotch tape test reveals oval eggs with a flattened side. The most likely organism is:
questions.explanation: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) causes perianal itching; diagnosis confirmed by identification of eggs on scotch tape test.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with fever, myalgia, and periorbital edema 3 weeks after eating undercooked pork. He has eosinophilia and elevated creatine kinase. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Trichinellosis follows ingestion of undercooked pork containing larvae; presents with fever, myalgia, periorbital edema, and eosinophilia.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain 2 weeks after returning from a trip to India. Ultrasound shows a solitary liver cyst with internal echoes. The most appropriate treatment is:
questions.explanation: Hydatid cyst (Echinococcus granulosus) is treated with albendazole to sterilize the cyst, followed by percutaneous drainage or surgery to remove the cyst.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and hemoptysis 6 months after returning from a trip to East Africa. Chest X-ray shows a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis is the most common cause of cavitary lung lesions worldwide; strongly associated with travel to endemic regions.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with fever, arthralgia, and a maculopapular rash that started on her wrists and ankles and spread centrally. She reports a tick bite 2 weeks ago. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Rocky Mountain spotted fever presents with fever, rash starting on wrists/ankles, and history of tick bite; caused by Rickettsia rickettsii.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with fever, abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea 2 days after attending a birthday party. Stool culture grows Shigella sonnei. The most appropriate antimicrobial therapy is:
options: Ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days
Metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days
questions.explanation: Azithromycin is recommended for Shigella infections in children due to increasing resistance to fluoroquinolones; duration is typically 3 days.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with fever, confusion, and a petechial rash after a camping trip. Blood cultures grow gram-negative coccobacilli. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Leptospirosis presents with fever, confusion, petechial rash, and exposure to contaminated water; diagnosis confirmed by blood culture or serology.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with fever, headache, and neck stiffness 1 week after returning from a safari in Kenya. Lumbar puncture shows 500 WBC/mm³ with 80% lymphocytes. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Viral meningitis typically presents with lymphocytic pleocytosis and milder clinical course; common after travel to tropical regions.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and hemoptysis 3 weeks after returning from a trip to South Sudan. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Melioidosis is endemic in Southeast Asia and northern Australia; presents with pneumonia, sepsis, and can mimic tuberculosis.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with fever, jaundice, and dark urine 2 weeks after returning from a trip to Uganda. Liver function tests show elevated bilirubin and transaminases. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Hepatitis A is transmitted via fecal-oral route and is common in travelers to endemic regions; presents with fever, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with fever, myalgia, and a macular rash that started on his trunk and spread to his extremities. He reports exposure to ticks during a hiking trip. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Ehrlichiosis presents with fever, myalgia, and rash after tick exposure; caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis or Anaplasma phagocytophilum.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with fever, cough, and weight loss 6 months after returning from a trip to Ethiopia. Chest X-ray shows a right upper lobe cavity. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis is the most common cause of cavitary lung lesions worldwide; strongly associated with travel to endemic regions.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with acute onset of fever, refusal to bear weight on his right leg, and localized warmth over the distal femur. His mother reports he had a minor knee injury while playing soccer 3 days ago. On examination, he is febrile (38.8°C), tachycardic, and appears toxic. Labs show WBC 16,000/mm³, CRP 85 mg/L, and ESR 55 mm/h. Blood cultures are pending. X-ray of the femur is normal.

modelAnswer.a: Most likely diagnosis: Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis of the distal femur.
modelAnswer.b: Pharmacological management: Empiric IV antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) such as vancomycin 15 mg/kg q8–12h or cloxacillin 50 mg/kg q6h. Duration: 4–6 weeks IV followed by oral therapy if clinical improvement.
modelAnswer.c: Non-pharmacological management: Rest, elevation of the limb, analgesia (paracetamol or ibuprofen), and orthopedic consultation for possible surgical drainage if abscess or failure to improve within 48–72 hours.
modelAnswer.d: Monitoring: Daily clinical assessment, CRP every 48–72 hours to assess response, repeat imaging (MRI or ultrasound) if no improvement.

questions.stem: Identify the most important member of Enterobacteriaceae responsible for each of the following clinical syndromes:

modelAnswer.d: Hemorrhagic colitis or Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS): Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC), particularly E. coli O157:H7

questions.stem: List three human worms (parasites) that can cause iron deficiency anemia and one parasite associated with pernicious anemia.

modelAnswer.i: Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) — causes vitamin B12 deficiency leading to megaloblastic anemia

questions.stem: Pablo, a 41-year-old security officer, is bitten by a neighbor’s dog while passing near the neighbor’s driveway. The dog’s vaccination history is unclear. Formulate an appropriate treatment plan for Pablo and include counseling points.

modelAnswer.i: Monitor wound for signs of infection (increased pain, redness, swelling, pus) and seek medical attention if these occur.
modelAnswer.ii: Complete the full course of rabies vaccine and return for all scheduled doses.
modelAnswer.iii: Report any adverse reactions to vaccines or antibiotics immediately.
modelAnswer.iv: Avoid contact with stray animals and report any animal bites to local health authorities.

questions.stem: Match each clinical presentation with the causative parasite:

modelAnswer.a: Intestinal obstruction and malnutrition in a child: Ascaris lumbricoides
modelAnswer.b: Perianal itching and insomnia: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm)
modelAnswer.c: Hepatomegaly, fever, and eosinophilia after freshwater exposure: Schistosoma mansoni
modelAnswer.d: Calabar swellings and microfilariae in blood: Loa loa

questions.stem: A 14-month-old child presents with 3 days of watery diarrhea, vomiting, and fever. The child is moderately dehydrated (6% fluid deficit). The mother reports the child has had 10 watery stools in the last 24 hours. The child is breastfeeding and also takes a cup of cow’s milk daily.

modelAnswer.a: Most likely diagnosis: Acute gastroenteritis with moderate dehydration due to viral or bacterial pathogen (e.g., rotavirus, norovirus, or Campylobacter).
modelAnswer.i: Rehydration: Oral rehydration solution (ORS) 75 mL/kg over 4 hours for moderate dehydration, then maintenance ORS.
modelAnswer.ii: Zinc supplementation: 20 mg/day for 10–14 days to reduce duration and severity of diarrhea.
modelAnswer.iii: Continue breastfeeding and age-appropriate diet (avoid milk if lactose intolerance suspected).
modelAnswer.iv: Monitor for signs of deterioration (increased lethargy, sunken eyes, poor urine output).
modelAnswer.c: Antimicrobial therapy: Not routinely indicated unless bacterial etiology confirmed (e.g., bloody diarrhea, high fever, or systemic toxicity). If Campylobacter suspected, azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day for 3 days.
modelAnswer.d: Prevention: Hand hygiene, safe food preparation, rotavirus vaccination if not previously administered.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with fever, joint pain, and a pustular rash on her arms and legs. She is sexually active with multiple partners and has no history of travel. On examination, she has tenosynovitis in the wrists and a temperature of 38.8°C. Labs show WBC 13.4 × 10⁹/L, CRP 318 mg/L, and ESR 96 mm/h.

modelAnswer.a: Most likely diagnosis: Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI).
modelAnswer.i: Blood cultures (positive in ~50% of DGI cases).
modelAnswer.ii: Synovial fluid analysis (if arthritis present) — Gram stain and culture for N. gonorrhoeae.
modelAnswer.iii: Urethral/cervical/rectal swabs for N. gonorrhoeae NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test).
modelAnswer.d: Treatment: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM/IV once daily for 7 days (or until clinical improvement), followed by azithromycin 1 g PO single dose for possible chlamydial co-infection.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents with fever, confusion, and a new macular rash on his trunk 10 days after returning from a rural area in Kenya. He reports exposure to stagnant water and ticks. Blood smear shows intraerythrocytic parasites.

modelAnswer.i: Uncomplicated P. falciparum: Artemether-lumefantrine 20/120 mg tablets (weight-based dosing) for 3 days.
modelAnswer.ii: Severe malaria: IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 hours, then daily until oral therapy tolerated.
modelAnswer.iii: Supportive care: Antipyretics, IV fluids if dehydration, monitor for complications (cerebral malaria, severe anemia).
